Statewide Mutual Insurance — Diminished Value Claims Policy (Auto)
A diminished value claim may be filed only when all of the following are met:
1. The claimant's vehicle was damaged in an accident caused by another party's negligence - this does not apply to at-fault claims or single-vehicle accidents.
2. The claim is made against the at-fault party's insurer (a third-party claim) - Statewide does not pay diminished value on its own policyholders' at-fault claims.
3. The vehicle is model year 2010 or newer and had fewer than 90,000 miles on the odometer at the time of loss.
4. The claim is filed within 2 years of the date of loss.
Vehicles that carried a salvage or rebuilt title prior to the accident are ineligible under any circumstance, regardless of the criteria above.

Kessler initially disputed fault, claiming Petrov 'stopped short,' but the police report cited Kessler for following too closely, and Kessler's own insurer (Statewide) accepted liability on his behalf after reviewing the dashcam footage Petrov provided.
Repair cost: $6,200, paid by Statewide under the property damage portion of Kessler's liability coverage. Repairs are complete; the vehicle shows no visible damage.

Summit Health Plan Appeals Process (Member Handbook Excerpt)
A member who disagrees with a claim denial must file an internal appeal within 180 days of the denial notice. Summit will respond to the internal appeal within 30 days (or 72 hours for urgent/expedited appeals involving ongoing treatment). If the internal appeal is denied, the member may request an external review by an independent review organization (IRO) within 4 months of the internal appeal denial. A member may not request external review before completing the internal appeal, except in cases where Summit fails to respond to the internal appeal within its required timeframe, in which case the member may proceed directly to external review. An appeal may be filed by the member directly, or by an authorized representative (such as a patient advocate or attorney) with the member's written consent on file. Appeals filed by a representative without consent on file will be returned unprocessed until consent is provided.

Claims log - Member: Harold Beck, Claim #CL-40217
- Feb 28: Claim for out-of-network surgery denied as 'not medically necessary.' Denial notice mailed March 1.
- Mar 20: Harold files internal appeal in writing, including a supporting letter from his surgeon.
- Mar 21: Summit's system logs the appeal as received, assigns case #AP-9944, target response date Apr 20 (30 days out).
- Apr 20: No response issued; internal ticket shows appeal still 'under physician review.'
- Apr 25: Harold's patient advocate, Teresa Nguyen, calls Summit for a status update. Harold's written consent authorizing Teresa as his representative has been on file with Summit since February.

Separately, Harold has an unrelated claim, #CL-40350 (a routine checkup denied for a billing code error), for which he filed an internal appeal on April 1; Summit's response isn't due until May 1, and no issue has arisen with that one.

Email from Teresa Nguyen (Patient Advocate) to Summit Appeals Dept, Apr 26:
'As Harold's authorized representative, following up on claim #CL-40217 / appeal #AP-9944. Per your own policy, internal appeals should be resolved within 30 days of filing - that deadline (Apr 20) has now passed with no decision. Harold would like to know whether he can proceed directly to external review given the missed deadline, or whether he must continue waiting for your internal decision.'

Email from Summit Appeals Dept to Teresa Nguyen, Apr 27:
'Thank you for reaching out. You are correct that our internal response deadline of Apr 20 has passed without a decision. Per our appeals policy, that allows Harold to request external review now, without waiting further for our internal decision. I'm attaching the external review request form. Separately, I'll flag internally that this case exceeded its response window - that's on us, not any action Harold needs to take.'

state:
Homestead Insurance HO-3 Policy: this policy provides 'open peril' (all-risk) coverage for the dwelling, covering all causes of loss except those specifically excluded. Excluded perils include: flood (surface water, storm surge, overflow of a body of water), earth movement, and neglect. Water damage from a sudden and accidental discharge or overflow of plumbing, heating, or AC systems WITHIN the home (e.g., a burst pipe) IS covered, even though flood is excluded, because it is not 'flood' as defined above - it is a covered sudden-discharge event, provided the homeowner acted promptly to prevent further damage upon discovery.

Adjuster file, Claim #HM-55291, policyholder Bethany Cole:

Incident summary (from homeowner's written statement): 'Overnight on the 14th, a supply line under my upstairs bathroom sink apparently burst. I didn't notice until I woke up around 7am and found water coming through the hallway ceiling below. I shut off the main water valve immediately, called a plumber (who came same day and replaced the line), and also called a water-mitigation company, who started drying equipment that afternoon. Damage: hallway ceiling drywall, some hallway flooring, and minor damage to a hallway closet. Separately - not sure if this matters for the claim - we also had a lot of rain that same week, and I noticed some water seeping in along the basement floor near the foundation wall, probably just from how saturated the ground got. I haven't done anything about that yet and I'm not asking to claim for it, just mentioning it in case it's related.'

Adjuster notes (Priya Osei):
- Confirmed cause of upstairs damage: sudden failure of a supply line fitting, not a gradual leak or neglect - the line showed no sign of prior corrosion or wear consistent with long-term seepage.
- Homeowner's response time (same-morning shutoff, same-day plumber and mitigation) satisfies the prompt-action requirement.
- Basement seepage: homeowner has NOT filed a claim for this; noting separately that groundwater seepage through a foundation from surface saturation would fall under the flood exclusion (surface water) if it were claimed, but that is not part of this claim.
- Recommend approving the hallway ceiling/flooring/closet damage under the sudden-discharge provision. Basement item noted for file only, no action, no claim submitted.

Phone call summary, Priya Osei with Bethany Cole, follow-up: Priya explained the upstairs damage is covered as a sudden discharge event given the quick response. Priya also mentioned that, for future reference, the basement seepage as described would likely fall under the flood exclusion if a claim were ever submitted for it, since it stems from surface water, not an internal plumbing failure - but reiterated no claim has been made for that and none is needed unless Bethany wants to pursue it separately (in which case a distinct flood policy, which Bethany does not have, would typically be needed).

state:
Meadowbrook Homeowners Policy: personal property claims are initially paid on an Actual Cash Value (ACV) basis (replacement cost minus depreciation). If the policyholder repairs or replaces the damaged item and submits proof of the completed replacement within 180 days of the ACV payment, the insurer pays the remaining 'recoverable depreciation' to bring the total payment up to full Replacement Cost Value (RCV). state:
Journey Shield Travel Insurance — Cancel For Any Reason (CFAR) Upgrade, Policy Section 7
CFAR is available only if purchased within 21 days of the initial trip deposit, and only if, at the time of purchase, the total trip cost is fully insured (100% of prepaid, non-refundable trip costs). If validly purchased, CFAR allows cancellation for any reason not otherwise covered, reimbursing 75% of the insured trip cost, provided the trip is cancelled at least 2 full days before the scheduled departure date. Cancelling within 2 days of departure forfeits CFAR benefits entirely, though the base policy's standard covered-reasons benefits may still apply if applicable.

Purchase record:
- Jan 5: initial trip deposit paid by Marcus and Elaine Henderson, total trip cost $8,000 (fully non-refundable per the tour operator's terms).
- Jan 20: the Hendersons purchase the base Journey Shield policy plus the CFAR upgrade, insuring the full $8,000 trip cost.
- Departure date: June 1.

Customer chat transcript, May 28:
Elaine Henderson: Hi, we need to cancel our June 1 trip. We just decided we'd rather not go anymore, nothing medical or anything, we just changed our minds about the destination.
Agent: I understand. Let me pull up your policy... I see you have the CFAR upgrade, purchased Jan 20, insuring the full $8,000 trip cost. Can you confirm today's date for our records?
Elaine Henderson: Today is May 28.
Agent: Thank you. And just to confirm, you're not cancelling for any of the standard covered reasons like illness, injury, or a covered event - just a personal change of plans?
Elaine Henderson: Right, just changed our minds, no covered reason.
Agent: Understood. Since you have a validly purchased CFAR upgrade, cancelling for 'change of mind' is exactly the kind of reason CFAR is designed to cover, since it's not one of the standard listed reasons. Let me just double check your departure date and cancellation date fall far enough apart... You're cancelling 4 days before your June 1 departure, which is outside the 2-day cutoff, so the CFAR reimbursement rate applies normally.
Elaine Henderson: Great, so what do we get back?
Agent: 75% of your insured trip cost of $8,000, which comes to $6,000.

Golden Oak Life Insurance: during the first 2 years after a policy is issued (the 'contestability period'), the insurer may investigate and deny a death claim, or rescind the policy, if it discovers a material misstatement on the application (e.g., undisclosed medical condition, false statement about smoking status) that would have affected underwriting. After the 2-year contestability period has elapsed, the policy becomes incontestable on these grounds, regardless of any misstatement discovered later, except in cases of proven fraud.

Case: policyholder Warren Blake died 26 months after his policy was issued. During the claim investigation, the insurer discovered Warren had failed to disclose a heart condition diagnosed shortly before applying; there is no evidence of intentional fraud, just an omission the insurer believes was a mistake or oversight.

questions.instruction: Can Golden Oak deny this claim based on the undisclosed heart condition?
questions.notes: 26 months exceeds the 2-year contestability period, and there is no proven fraud.

questions.instruction: Why can't Golden Oak use the undisclosed condition to deny this claim?

candidates.description: The 2-year contestability period has already passed and there is no proven fraud
The condition was actually disclosed on the application
The condition would not have affected underwriting
The insurer already waived its right to review claims

questions.notes: 26 months post-issue places this outside the 2-year window, with no proven fraud alleged.

questions.instruction: Would the outcome be different if Warren had died 20 months after the policy was issued instead of 26?
questions.notes: 20 months would fall within the 2-year contestability period, allowing investigation and possible denial.

questions.instruction: Which of the following are true about this claim?

candidates.description: More than 2 years have passed since the policy was issued
The insurer has proven intentional fraud
Warren failed to disclose a medical condition on his application
The claim can be denied based on this undisclosed condition

questions.notes: No fraud is proven, and without it the past-contestability claim can't be denied on this basis.

state:
Golden Oak Life Insurance: the death benefit is paid to the primary beneficiary(ies) named on the policy. If a primary beneficiary predeceases the insured, that beneficiary's share passes to the contingent beneficiary(ies), UNLESS the policy designates the beneficiary's share as 'per stirpes,' in which case that deceased beneficiary's share instead passes to their own children (the insured's grandchildren, or other named heirs), bypassing the contingent beneficiary entirely for that share.

Case: the policyholder named his two children, Anna and Ben, as primary beneficiaries (50% each, designated 'per stirpes'), and his brother as sole contingent beneficiary. Anna predeceased the policyholder, leaving two children of her own (the policyholder's grandchildren). Ben is still living.

questions.instruction: Who receives Anna's 50% share of the death benefit?

candidates.description: Ben, the surviving co-primary beneficiary
The policyholder's brother, the contingent beneficiary
Anna's own children, per stirpes
The policyholder's estate

questions.notes: The per stirpes designation redirects her share to her own children.

questions.instruction: Does the policyholder's brother receive any part of the death benefit in this scenario?
questions.notes: Per stirpes bypasses the contingent beneficiary entirely for Anna's share; Ben's share is unaffected and stays with Ben.

questions.instruction: Does Ben still receive his 50% share?
questions.notes: Ben is living; only Anna's share is redirected.

state:
Golden Oak Life Insurance — Accidental Death Benefit (Double Indemnity) Rider
If the insured's death results directly from an accident (not disease or natural causes), the rider pays an additional death benefit equal to the base policy's face value (i.e., double the total payout). The rider excludes deaths resulting from: self-inflicted injury, participation in an illegal activity (a felony), intoxication (blood alcohol over the legal driving limit at the time of the accident, if driving), or voluntary intake of any controlled substance not prescribed by a doctor. Death must occur within 90 days of the accident for the rider to apply.

Claims Investigation Report, Claim #AD-77210. Insured: Todd Marsh | Face value: $200,000 | Rider: Accidental Death Benefit (Double Indemnity).

Incident summary: on March 3, Todd Marsh was involved in a single-car accident when his vehicle's rear tire blew out on the highway, causing him to lose control and strike a guardrail. He was hospitalized with severe injuries and died on March 15 (12 days after the accident) from complications related to his injuries.

Toxicology and police findings:
- Blood alcohol content at the time of the crash: 0.05%, below the state's 0.08% legal driving limit.
- State police investigation concluded the proximate cause of the accident was a tire blowout due to a manufacturing defect, not driver impairment or error.
- No citations or charges were issued to Todd in connection with the accident.
- No controlled substances (prescribed or otherwise) were found in his system.

Claims examiner conclusion (Rosalind Kim): 'Reviewing this claim against our accidental death rider exclusions: Todd's BAC was under the legal limit, so the intoxication exclusion does not apply. Police attributed the accident to a mechanical defect, not any illegal activity, so the illegal-activity exclusion doesn't apply either. No controlled substances were involved. Death occurred 12 days after the accident, well within the 90-day window. This death qualifies as accidental under the rider - recommend approving the double indemnity payout of an additional $200,000, for a total payout of $400,000.'

Email from attorney Denise Whitfield (representing the beneficiary) to Rosalind Kim: 'Thank you for the update. Just to make sure I understand for the file - if his BAC had instead been measured at 0.09%, would that have changed the outcome even though police didn't find impairment caused the accident?'

Email from Rosalind Kim to Denise Whitfield: 'Good question. Per the rider language, the intoxication exclusion is based on the BAC threshold itself at the time of the accident while driving, not on whether intoxication was the proven cause of the crash. So yes - a BAC of 0.09%, being over the 0.08% limit, would trigger the exclusion regardless of what actually caused the accident, and the double indemnity portion would not be payable in that scenario. The base policy's ordinary death benefit would still be payable either way, since that's unrelated to this rider.'

questions.instruction: Does Todd's death qualify for the double indemnity payout?
questions.notes: His BAC was under the limit, the cause was mechanical, no substances involved, and death was within 90 days.

questions.instruction: Which of the following exclusion criteria were investigated and ruled out for this claim?

candidates.description: Intoxication (BAC over the legal limit while driving)
Participation in an illegal activity
Voluntary intake of an unprescribed controlled substance
Self-inflicted injury

questions.notes: The report never addresses self-inflicted injury at all, so it can't be confirmed as ruled out.

questions.instruction: Was Todd's death within the 90-day window required for the rider to apply?
questions.notes: He died 12 days after the accident.

questions.instruction: If Todd's BAC had been 0.09% instead of 0.05%, would the double indemnity portion still be payable?
questions.notes: 0.09% exceeds the 0.08% threshold, triggering the intoxication exclusion regardless of actual cause.
